title: How to program a Gentleman split
summary: NH lays out how to build the skeleton of a gentleman split: choose 4-5 training days, use an upper/lower structure with flexible boundaries, name each day by its main movement pattern and target muscles, and build accessories around the compound lift. He warns against greed turning it into a full body, stresses choosing exercises in advance, and introduces alpha/beta testing of programs.
claims: The gentleman split is his favorite template: an upper/lower skeleton combined with body-part-split elements, prized for its flexibility
Training 2 days or 7 days per week does not work for a gentleman split (too low frequency and too much volume per day, or requiring extreme volume tolerance)
3 and 6 days per week are the sub-extreme range; 3 days leaves you one day short and novices do not need this advanced structure
He trains 6 days, which suits rare people who respond extremely well to volume, have poor strength leverages and are injury prone in certain rep ranges, so they need more days to accumulate volume
The optimal range is 4-5 days per week, with 4 closest to ideal
Upper/lower is the best skeleton: it saves warm-up time, prevents injury and groups synergistic muscles
Lower body compounds do not activate the upper body enough to count as tonnage and vice versa, e.g. leg drive on the bench
Boundaries are flexible: calves can go on an upper day and upper back on a lower day
Name each day by its main movement pattern and its target muscles; he finds starting from movement patterns easiest
A day must be justified by a compound lift; a triceps-only day is a bro split, and no heavy compound recruits only one muscle
A starter bench day: horizontal press, vertical press, then a chest or shoulder accessory, covering chest, triceps and shoulders
To add biceps to a pressing day, use band curls (easy on tendons) or chin-ups, which also add upper back work
Do not be greedy adding muscles to a day or it becomes a full body workout; full body rarely digs deep enough per muscle, fine for novices but not for massive gains
A squat-based lower day covers quads, glutes, hamstrings and lower back, with room for calves, core and upper back
Upper back fits on any day and can handle massive volume if you know how to train it
Decide exercise selection before programming so lifts are synergistic, never on the spot
The week is a human invention; arrange the four days in whatever pattern fits your recovery from volume and intensity
Start a new program slightly under-ambitious; alpha test then beta test it, making modifications during the beta, then cruise on it; never run an untested program unmodified
exercises: dips and push-ups also count as the horizontal press
adds biceps to a push day, easy on the tendons
adds biceps plus upper back to an upper day
anchors a lower day for quads, glutes, hamstrings, lower back
vertical press to stack on the upper day
